nameStory: The 'beggarticks' name comes from this plant's notorious habit of hitching a ride on anyone who passes by. Its seeds have barbed tips that grab onto clothing, fur, and socks like tiny beggars clinging to passersby, refusing to let go until they've found a new place to grow.
description: Bearded Beggarticks is a cheerful annual wildflower that looks like a smaller, more delicate sunflower. It grows 1-4 feet tall with bright yellow daisy-like flowers that have 6-10 showy petals surrounding a golden center. The plant has deeply divided, feathery leaves that give it a lacy appearance, and it blooms from late summer into fall when many other flowers are fading.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers about 1-2 inches across with 6-10 broad, notched petals that feel papery to the touch, surrounding a darker yellow center disk

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided leaves that feel soft and slightly fuzzy, cut into narrow segments that create a feathery, lace-like pattern

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Dark brown, flattened seeds topped with 2-4 sharp, backward-pointing barbs that feel prickly and stick tenaciously to fabric and fur

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, branching plant that forms loose colonies in wet areas, with multiple flower heads clustered at the tips of branches

habitat: Look for Bearded Beggarticks in wet meadows, marsh edges, and along stream banks where the soil stays moist. It thrives in disturbed areas like roadside ditches and the edges of ponds, often growing alongside cattails, jewelweed, and other moisture-loving plants.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring, but plants remain small and inconspicuous during early growth.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly through summer, developing their characteristic feathery foliage but not yet flowering.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming occurs from August through October, when bright yellow flowers create showy displays. Seeds mature and become sticky hitchhikers by late fall.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist with empty seed heads, but the annual plants have completed their life cycle.

funFact: This plant is like nature's velcro inventor - its barbed seeds inspired part of the design for modern hook-and-loop fasteners, and a single plant can produce over 3,000 hitchhiking seeds that can stick to your clothes and travel for miles!
confusionNotes: It's easily confused with other beggarticks species, but Bearded Beggarticks is the showiest of the bunch with the largest, most prominent yellow petals. Memory trick: it's the 'beautiful beggar' - if the flowers are big and showy, you've found the bearded one.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being native to the central United States, this species has become naturalized in parts of New England where it's sometimes considered weedy. Its many common names reflect its widespread distribution - it's called 'Yankee lice' in some regions, a rather unflattering reference to its clingy seeds.
compareHints: Among New England's beggarticks, Bearded Beggarticks stands out for its large, showy yellow petals - most other species like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all. It's also distinguished by its deeply cut, almost ferny leaves, while relatives like Nodding Beggarticks have simple, lance-shaped leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Devil's Beggarticks is distinguished by its three-part leaves (versus simple leaves in Nodding Beggarticks) and its lack of showy petals (unlike the bright yellow rays of Tickseed Sunflower).

Among New England's many beggarticks species, Nodding Beggarticks is the easiest to identify because of its drooping flowers - Devil's Beggarticks has upward-facing flowers and deeply divided leaves, while Smooth Beggarticks has much larger, showier flowers that face outward.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Purplestem stands out for its smooth stems with purple coloring and relatively few flower heads per plant.
Unlike its weedy beggarticks relatives that grow in damp soil and are known for their sticky seeds, Water Marigold is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Among New England's beggarticks, Tall Beggarticks stands out for its height and hairy stems.

Unlike its freshwater cousins like Devil's Beggarticks or Nodding Beggarticks, Estuary Beggarticks has evolved to handle salt stress, giving it thicker, more succulent leaves and limiting it to coastal habitats.

Among its many Bidens relatives in New England, Smooth Beggarticks stands out for its simple, undivided leaves (unlike Three-parted Beggarticks) and its prominent yellow ray petals (unlike Devil's Beggarticks which often lacks showy petals entirely).

Among its many beggarticks relatives, swamp beggarticks stands out for its complete lack of ray petals (the showy outer petals), unlike nodding beggarticks or smooth beggarticks which have yellow rays.

Among New England beggarticks, Three-parted is unique for its deeply three-divided leaves - Devil's Beggarticks has simple oval leaves, while Spanish Needles has finely divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Tickseed Sunflower stands out for having showy yellow petals - many of its relatives like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Among its beggarticks relatives, Spanish needles stands out with its finely divided, feathery leaves - most other Bidens species have simple oval leaves or leaves divided into just 3-5 broad segments.

Marsh Tickseed stands out from its beggarticks relatives by being strictly a wetland specialist - while cousins like Devil's Beggarticks grow in disturbed soils and gardens, Marsh Tickseed demands consistently soggy conditions.
Among its many beggarticks relatives, Eaton's is unique for its salt marsh habitat - most others prefer freshwater wetlands or disturbed soils.
White beggarticks stands out from its many beggarticks relatives because of its prominent white petals - most other species in the genus have small, inconspicuous flowers or yellow petals.
